title: 9 Types of Logos Explained
author: arek-dvornechuck-ebaqdesign

seo.title: 9 Types of Logos Explained With 27 Examples
seo.description: The 9 types of logos explained by a brand designer, with 27 real examples: wordmarks, lettermarks, letterforms, pictorial and abstract marks, mascots, combination marks, emblems and dynamic logos.

description: The 9 types of logos explained by a brand designer, with 27 real examples: wordmarks, lettermarks, letterforms, pictorial and abstract marks, mascots, combination marks, emblems and dynamic logos.
intro:
There are 9 types of logos: wordmarks, lettermarks, letterforms, pictorial marks, abstract marks, mascots, combination marks, emblems and dynamic logos. Most lists stop at seven. I add letterforms and dynamic logos because more and more brands use them, especially in tech, where a logo has to work as a tiny app icon.

Logo design quick course: this is the overview of my series on logo types. Go deeper with emblem logos, script logos, mascot logos, wordmark logos, lettermark logos, monogram logos and abstract logos.

I'm a brand designer, and choosing the type of logo is one of the first decisions I make with every client. It decides how the brand reads on a sign, a shoebox and a phone screen. Below, each type has a plain definition, when to use it, what to watch out for and three famous examples, each on a slide with my handwritten notes.

The 9 types of logos at a glance

The nine types fall into three groups. Text logos (wordmarks, lettermarks and letterforms) are built from letters. Symbol logos (pictorial marks, abstract marks and mascots) are built from a picture. Combined logos (combination marks, emblems and dynamic logos) mix the two, or change over time.

  1. Wordmark: the full name in type, like Coca-Cola
  2. Lettermark: initials, like IBM
  3. Letterform: a single letter, like the McDonald's M
  4. Pictorial mark: a picture of a real thing, like the Apple apple
  5. Abstract mark: a shape with no literal meaning, like the Nike Swoosh
  6. Mascot logo: a character, like KFC's Colonel
  7. Combination mark: a symbol plus the name, like Puma
  8. Emblem: the name inside a badge, like Harley-Davidson
  9. Dynamic logo: a logo that changes, like Google Doodles

faq.question: What are the main types of logos?
faq.answer: The nine types of logos are wordmarks, lettermarks, letterforms, pictorial marks, abstract marks, mascots, combination marks, emblems and dynamic logos. Many guides list seven, leaving out letterforms and dynamic logos.

faq.question: What are the 7 types of logos?
faq.answer: The classic seven are wordmarks, lettermarks, pictorial marks, abstract marks, mascots, combination marks and emblems. Letterforms, like the McDonald's M, and dynamic logos, like Google Doodles, are two newer types that are worth knowing.

faq.question: Which type of logo is best for a new business?
faq.answer: For most new businesses, a combination mark is the safest choice. The name builds recognition while the symbol earns its place, and the symbol can be used alone later, for example as an app icon.

faq.question: What is the difference between a combination mark and an emblem?
faq.answer: In a combination mark, the symbol and the name sit next to each other and can be separated, like Puma's cat and wordmark. In an emblem, the name sits inside the shape and can't be separated, like the Harley-Davidson bar and shield.

faq.question: What is the difference between a wordmark and a lettermark?
faq.answer: A wordmark spells out the full brand name, like Coca-Cola or Visa. A lettermark uses only the initials, like IBM, HBO or CNN.

faq.question: How much does a professional logo cost?
faq.answer: Prices vary a lot by designer. I design a complete brand identity, including the logo and its simpler versions, in one week for a flat $3,000.

body:
1. Wordmark

A wordmark is the brand name set in custom or carefully chosen type, with no symbol. The letters are the logo.

Best for: Short, distinctive names that you want people to remember and spell.

Watch out for: Long or generic names, and app icons, where a full word gets too small to read.

Coca-Cola

Frank M. Robinson, the company's bookkeeper, wrote the Coca-Cola name in Spencerian script in 1886.

The flowing script is so distinctive that it doesn't need a symbol.

FedEx

Lindon Leader at Landor designed the FedEx wordmark in 1994, hiding an arrow between the E and the x.

Plain bold letters, with one smart detail you can't unsee once you spot it.

Visa

BankAmericard became Visa in 1976, a short name that reads the same in many languages.

Four italic capitals lean forward, like the brand is in motion.

Go deeper: more wordmark examples and how to design one.

2. Lettermark

A lettermark shortens a long name to its initials. IBM is easier to say and print than International Business Machines.

Best for: Long company names that people already shorten in conversation.

Watch out for: New brands. Initials mean nothing until people know what they stand for.

IBM

Paul Rand added the horizontal stripes to the IBM logo in 1972, to suggest speed and dynamism.

Eight stripes turn three heavy letters into something lighter and faster.

HBO

HBO stands for Home Box Office, and its logo has kept the O drawn like a camera lens since the 1970s.

The O becomes a lens, the one detail that hints at film.

CNN

Anthony Guy Bost designed the CNN logo in 1980, with a cable running through the letters.

One continuous line links the three letters, like a TV cable.

Go deeper: more lettermark examples and how to design one.

3. Letterform

A letterform logo uses a single letter, usually the first letter of the name, drawn as a strong shape.

Best for: App icons, favicons and brands that need one bold, square symbol.

Watch out for: Letters are hard to own. Many brands share the same initial.

McDonald's

Jim Schindler, McDonald's head of engineering and design, turned the arches on the restaurants into an M in 1962.

The M started as architecture: two golden arches on the roof.

Netflix

Netflix added the red N symbol in 2016, so the brand would fit app icons and small screens.

Shadows make the N look like a folded ribbon.

Tesla

Elon Musk said in 2017 that the Tesla T stands for part of a cross section of an electric motor.

The T doubles as a piece of the machine the company builds.

Go deeper: more letterform examples and how to design one.

4. Pictorial mark

A pictorial mark is a picture of a real thing: an apple, a shell, a target. People name it the moment they see it.

Best for: Brands with a simple name-to-picture link, or a name people already know.

Watch out for: Pictures that lock you into one product as the business grows.

Apple

Rob Janoff designed the Apple logo in 1977; the bite keeps the apple from looking like a cherry.

A real object, made unique by one bite.

Shell

Shell has used a seashell since 1904, and Raymond Loewy drew the current pecten in 1971.

The name is the picture, so the logo works without words.

Target

Target opened its first store in Roseville, Minnesota, in 1962 with a bullseye logo.

A literal target for a store called Target.

5. Abstract mark

An abstract mark is a shape that doesn't show a real object. It means whatever the brand teaches people it means.

Best for: Global brands that need a symbol that works in every language.

Watch out for: Small budgets. An abstract shape needs time and money before people link it to you.

Nike

Carolyn Davidson, a student at Portland State, designed the Nike Swoosh in 1971 for $35.

A tick of movement that means nothing on its own, and everything after 50 years.

Mastercard

Pentagram redesigned the interlocking circles in 2016, and in 2019 Mastercard dropped the name from the logo.

Two circles and an overlap: simple enough to read with no words.

Adidas

Peter Moore designed the three bars for the adidas Equipment line, released in 1991.

Three slanted bars echo the three stripes and suggest a mountain to climb.

Go deeper: more abstract mark examples and how to design one.

6. Mascot logo

A mascot logo puts a character in the logo: a person, an animal or a made-up creature with a face.

Best for: Food, kids' brands and apps that want a friendly voice.

Watch out for: Fine detail that turns to mush at small sizes, and characters that age badly.

KFC

KFC's first logo put Colonel Harland Sanders' face on the sign in 1952, and a 2026 redesign by JKR turned the bucket stripes into the letters K, F and C.

A real founder's face makes the chicken feel like one man's recipe.

Michelin

Poster artist O'Galop drew Bibendum, the Michelin Man, in 1898 from a stack of tyres.

The character is built from the product itself.

Duolingo

Duolingo's in-house team redrew Duo the owl in 2019 to make him easier to animate.

Simple shapes let the owl move, react and nag in the app.

Go deeper: more mascot logo examples and how to design one.

7. Combination mark

A combination mark pairs a symbol with the brand name. The two can be used together or apart.

Best for: Most new businesses. The name builds recognition while the symbol earns its place.

Watch out for: Lockups that only work together. Design the symbol to stand alone from the start.

Puma

Nuremberg cartoonist Lutz Backes drew the leaping Puma cat in 1968.

The cat and the name work together, and the cat also works alone on a shoe.

Lacoste

Lacoste took its crocodile from the nickname of its founder, tennis player René Lacoste, and the croc went on his shirts in 1933.

A serif name and a small croc: classic, with one bit of fun.

Chase

Chermayeff & Geismar designed the Chase octagon in 1961 for Chase Manhattan Bank.

The octagon is abstract, the wordmark is plain, and together they're a combination mark.

8. Emblem

An emblem puts the name inside a shape: a badge, a shield, a seal or a crest. The name and the shape can't be separated.

Best for: Schools, sports teams, cars, beer and heritage brands.

Watch out for: Small text inside the shape that disappears on screens and embroidery.

Harley-Davidson

Harley-Davidson was founded in Milwaukee in 1903 and first used the bar and shield in 1910.

The name sits inside a shield and a bar, like a badge on a fuel tank.

BMW

BMW registered its roundel in 1917, and its blue and white quarters come from the colours of Bavaria.

The letters and the circle can't be separated, which is what makes it an emblem.

NFL

The NFL redrew its shield in 2008 with eight stars, one for each division, and a football on top.

Stars, a football and the letters packed into one shield.

Go deeper: more emblem examples and how to design one.

9. Dynamic logo

A dynamic logo changes. The colours, patterns or shapes shift while a fixed structure keeps it recognisable.

Best for: Cultural institutions, cities, media and tech brands with lots of content.

Watch out for: Weak rules. Without a fixed core, a dynamic logo stops looking like one brand.

Google

Larry Page and Sergey Brin drew the first Google Doodle in 1998, a stick figure behind the second o to show they were at Burning Man.

The wordmark is fixed, but the Doodles turn it into a new picture almost every day.

MIT Media Lab

Pentagram's Michael Bierut designed the MIT Media Lab logo in 2014 on a 7 by 7 grid, with a different glyph for each research group.

One grid, many symbols: the system is the logo.

City of Melbourne

Landor designed the City of Melbourne's faceted M in 2009, which can be filled with endless patterns.

The M keeps its shape while the fill changes for every use.

How to choose the right type of logo

Start with your name, not with a style you like. These four questions settle most projects:

1. How long is your name? A short, distinctive name like Visa or Google can carry a wordmark on its own. A long name like International Business Machines needs a lettermark or a symbol.

2. Where will people see it most? If your logo lives on an app icon or a social avatar, you need a square symbol or a single letter. If it lives on trucks, shopfronts and packaging, a wide wordmark works.

3. How well known are you? A symbol only works without a name once people already know it. Nike, Apple and Mastercard dropped their names only after decades of advertising. New brands should keep the name next to the symbol.

4. What is your budget for building recognition? Abstract marks and dynamic logos need time and money before they mean anything. A wordmark or a pictorial mark starts working on day one.

If you are still unsure, choose a combination mark. It gives you a name that people can read today and a symbol that can work alone later. That is what I recommend to most of my clients.

Most brands use more than one type

The types aren't boxes you choose once. A good identity is a logo system: a main logo plus simpler versions for small spaces. Chase uses its full combination mark on branches and just the octagon in its app. Netflix uses its wordmark on screens and the N as its app icon. KFC uses the Colonel with the name on buckets and the Colonel alone on cups. Plan the full system from the start, so every version looks like it belongs.

Logo types vs logo styles

A logo type is about what the logo is made of: letters, a picture, a character or a mix. A logo style is about how it looks. Script, minimalist, vintage, geometric and gradient are styles. A script logo like Coca-Cola is a wordmark in a handwritten style. A circle logo can be an emblem or an abstract mark. Techniques like negative space and symmetry work with any type: the FedEx arrow is negative space inside a wordmark.

Need help choosing the right type of logo?

Every type of logo can work. Wordmarks build the name, lettermarks shorten it, letterforms fit an app icon, pictures and abstract shapes cross languages, mascots add a personality, combination marks give you flexibility, emblems add heritage and dynamic logos keep a brand fresh. The right choice depends on your name, where people will see your logo and how much time you have to build recognition.
